title: Fixing things together
context: You will hear an interview with Marta Ruiz, who started a network of repair cafés where people fix broken things.

unit.style: a natural radio interview, warm and articulate, at a normal pace

turns.text: My guest today is Marta Ruiz, who started the first repair café in her city five years ago. There are now more than thirty. Marta, for anyone who hasn't been to one, what exactly is a repair café?

It's very simple, really. Once a month, we take over a community hall, and people bring in things that are broken: toasters, bicycles, jackets with broken zips, lamps. Volunteers with the right skills help them fix them. The important word there is help. We don't take your toaster away and give it back repaired. You sit next to the volunteer and do as much of the work as you can yourself.
Why does that matter so much?

Because the point isn't just to save one toaster. It's to change how people feel about the things they own. When you've opened something up and seen how it works, you're far less likely to throw it away the next time it goes wrong. A lot of people arrive convinced they're useless with their hands, and they leave feeling slightly proud of themselves.
How did it all start for you?

Rather by accident. My washing machine broke, and the company told me that repairing it would cost more than buying a new one. That seemed absurd to me, so I found a video online and fixed it myself for the price of a small part. I was so pleased that I told everyone I knew, and a neighbour suggested we organise something for the whole street.
Do manufacturers make repairs deliberately difficult?

Some do, although it's getting better. The biggest problem we see isn't products designed to fail; it's products that are glued together instead of screwed, so you can't get inside without breaking them. And spare parts can be impossible to find. New rules in Europe are starting to change that, which is encouraging, but there's a long way to go.

All sorts, but a surprising number are retired engineers and electricians who miss using their skills. We also get students, which I love, because the older volunteers enjoy passing on what they know. Some of our best friendships have started over a broken radio.
And what's the most unusual thing anyone has brought in?

Oh, that's easy. A man once arrived with a mechanical toy monkey that played the drums. It had belonged to his father, and it hadn't worked for sixty years. It took three volunteers an entire afternoon, but when it finally started playing again, half the room was in tears. Moments like that remind me that people aren't really attached to objects. They're attached to the memories that come with them.

Of course. Not everything can be saved, and we're honest about that. But even when a repair fails, people usually understand why their machine stopped working, and that changes what they look for next time. Several people have told me they now check whether a product can be repaired before they buy it, which is exactly the kind of change we hoped for.
Finally, what would you say to people who think repairing things is old-fashioned?
I'd say that throwing things away is what's old-fashioned. We simply can't afford to keep buying new things every time something breaks. Repairing isn't about going backwards. It's about growing up.
